newsitem.title: UK: Britain tells EU it will not drop work week fight.
newsitem.headline: Britain tells EU it will not drop work week fight.

text.p: Britain's John Major on Tuesday vowed to continue a fight for changes to European law after the European Court of Justice rejected a British challenge to a Brussels directive on a maximum working hours.
Speaking just after the court announced its ruling, Major said: "I believe it is a bad piece of legislation. I don't accept that it is appropriate to the United Kingdom."

Repeating his vow to fight the ruling made in a speech on Monday evening, he told reporters outside his Downing Street office: "We shall go to the IGC (inter-governmental conference) and insist on reversing this legislation."
British industrialists attacked the ruling -- which will limit the working week to 48 hours -- saying it would add to some of industry's costs.

In Monday's speech, Major said Britain would demand treaty changes before agreeing to any reforms being discussed as part of the IGC -- designed to streamline the EU's decision-making -- which is scheduled to finish in the middle of next year.
Trade and Industry Minister Ian Lang said Major had written to EU Commission President Jacques Santer on Tuesday to press Britain's case "in the most unequivocal terms".
The ruling Conservatives, trailing the opposition Labour party badly in opinion polls with an election due within six months, are bitterly split on Europe.
Major has been forced to take a tough line against Brussels to placate right-wingers in his party ranks who are bitterly opposed to any moves towards further European integration.
The opposition accused Major of trying to use the case to artificially stoke up anti-European sentiment in the run-up to the general election now no more than six months away.

Labour's David Blunkett said: "It is artificial indignation from a government that is...trying to use what are very modest measures to protect the rights of the individual in a way that they hope will create an anti-European feeling.
"It won't damage competitiveness. It will help to have a civilised society," said Blunkett, Labour employment spokesman.

Desp"ite the opposition of some British industrialists, unions largely welcomed it. John Monks, the general secretary of the umbrella Trade Union Congress (TUC) said: "I think this is very good news for British workers... this is a major contribution by the European Union."
Lang said in a statement Britain would obey the law until it could secure treaty changes to close what he called the "loophole" which allowed the directive to be introduced.

Major is angry the directive was brought in under European health and safety provisions -- provisions which allowed Britain to be outvoted by its European partners. He argued the issue has nothing to do with health and safety, and was wrongly adopted.
But, signalling the government's attempt to drag out the process, Lang added: "We will only legislate after carrying out full public consultation on the issues and options.

"In doing so we will aim to take advantage of the valuable derogations already secured and to preserve as much as possible of the flexibility that has been such an important element in the revival of the economy over recent years."
Britain has recently attracted the lion's share of overseas investment into the European Union because of its low wage costs and lack of labour regulations.
